utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. Today is the 1st of April, 2010. I would like to greet the witness. I would also like to greet Mr. Coric as well as Mr. Stojic and Mr. Prlic. I would also like to greet those who are not here today for various reasons, including for health reasons, and I wish that they get well soon. They have a few days to get better and to be back in good health so that they will attend the next hearings. And as you know, they will resume on Monday the 12th of April. The Prosecutor has 18 minutes left, so I give her the floor immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but might I be allowed to say something briefly before the Prosecutor goes ahead. I wanted to say at the beginning that I wish to apologise to the Trial Chamber, to the Prosecutor, and everybody else in the courtroom, because I got up at one point yesterday and I was hasty in saying that with respect to Witness Buntic I had shown the judgement from a trial relating to the four persons who were convicted of rape. However, it was the indictment and Prosecutor's lists, and I checked this out. I relied on my memory and thought it was perfect. However, when I got to my feet, I found that it was not perfect and I mixed two cases up. So I wanted to say that straight away to avoid any misunderstanding in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President. Good afternoon Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Vidovic. Yesterday, when we left off, we were talking about the Convicts Battalion, and you had indicated that there had not been an order from Mr. Coric not to arrest certain members of the group for fear of breaking them up, but, rather, you were arresting them as they committed crimes because - and I'm going to quote what you said yesterday at page 93: "We were preparing a larger-scale operation which would result in their arrest and a filing of a large number of criminal reports." Sir, do you remember that testimony from yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, in May of 1993, Juka Prazina was an HVO commander in Mostar, was he not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That he was the commander of the HVO in Mostar, is that what you're asking? I don't know that he was a commander. I have no knowledge of that post, that he was commander of the entire HVO. No, that's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What I actually said was a commander. So he was in the HVO, and he was a soldier in Mostar in May of 1993; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Was he ever prosecuted as a result of an investigation conducted by the Mostar crime investigative services?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, may we go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, I'm going to show you part of a transcript. And this is P03112. It will appear on the screen. This is a meeting; you didn't attend this meeting. Nonetheless, I'd like to talk about it to see if it helps in this discussion.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I could just have a moment, Your Honour. Thank you. This is July 2nd, 1993. It's a presidential transcript. And President Tudjman of Croatia says in it: "I knew that some of our people might be extremists, but I also knew that we could not eliminate such people due to the situation. If we had eliminated them, we would have jeopardised our position in Bosnia and Herzegovina."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do apologise, but could we have the transcript page from which the Prosecutor is reading so that we can see the context that Mr. Tudjman is saying what he is? Because to have an excerpt from a transcript page in this way and just look at one sentence can lead to a misunderstanding. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems that it's page 21 of the transcript of the 2nd of July, 1993. It's on the screen. It's page 21. Isn't it, Ms. West?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, Mr. Vidovic, my question to you is this: This theme, this theme of allowing extremists to operate unchecked in the HVO in order to support the goal of a purely Croatian Herceg-Bosna, this was a theme that was emanating from the very top, was it not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I wouldn't put it -- actually, this isn't my area, so I don't -- I don't want to discuss it in this way. I can't say what was discussed at the very top, the leadership of the State of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really wouldn't like to comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Yesterday and the day before, we had been speaking about a rape investigation, one that we -- counsel for Mr. Coric has just commented upon, and not to beat a dead horse, but if we could just look at P11240, and it should be right in front of you. P11240. It's loose. This is February 25th, 1997, and this is a verdict for three people and that they were acquitted. This is Mario Busic, Mario Coric, Mario Pazin, that they were acquitted. And also it notes that Blasko Knezovic's case had been terminated in 1995. Sir, looking at this acquittal now, does this help your memory in regard to what actually happened in this case?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This one? May I take a moment to read it, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise, but I think my learned friend made a mistake. The case wasn't over in 1985 [as interpreted], but we see that the judgement was made in February 1997 - am I right? - the first instance judgement. Because the date in the transcript is 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I'm sure there's just a mistranslation. This is from 1997, and the case against the fourth defendant as reflected on page 3 and 4 of the English was terminated in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir, does this help you remember that these four individuals were not convicted and were not sentenced? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just read through it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, if I may, while the gentleman is reading this. Yesterday, as I understood, the line of questioning was: Nothing happened to the men. Now, in the former Yugoslavia and then later on in Bosnia-Herzegovina, back in 1997, as is today, the presumption of innocence still exists. Thank God. And also, courts are functioning, at this point in time, 1997, OHR was there; Mostar was under international supervision; the courts were being monitored. There seems to have been a trial proceeding where people were acquitted. People are acquitted all over the world every day, again, based on the evidence. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Karnavas, what's the justification for you commenting and pleading on this?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: If I may be heard. [Overlapping speakers]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: The Chamber knows the law and is absolutely able to interpret what is brought before it. And there is time for pleading at the end, Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: This is not pleading. If I may be allowed to finish, Mr. President. The point that I'm trying to make is as follows: This is -- yesterday, the questioning was: Nothing was done. Today we see that something was done. That's the point that I'm trying to make. So she's not trying to remind him whether he had a recollection whether they were acquitted. That's the point. It's a point about being precise and being fair to the witness, Your Honour. And I dare say that it's my obligation to raise that and make a record of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: If I can just have a moment just to be absolutely --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I think I'll just remind the Court that the witness's testimony on direct was that these individuals had been convicted and sentenced.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And so, Mr. Vidovic, you have to indulge me. I can't give you any more time, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, thank you for this clarification, but I would like to come back to what Mr. Karnavas just said. I thought I understood that nothing had been done; and this document proves that things were done, that a trial was organised, and that the accused were acquitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think we have a bit of a disagreement here. As I said before, the gentleman's testimony on direct was that they were convicted and sentenced. What I'm trying to do is impeach that testimony. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: So, sir, again, not to beat a dead horse --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, this shows that they were acquitted; correct? This piece of paper in front of you --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what I can see in the document, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you. And, Mr. Vidovic, isn't it true that every criminal report you wrote up or your people wrote up did not result in a prosecution and conviction? Isn't that true? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour, but I have a small objection, and this is it: Perhaps the witness should first be asked how a policeman could know what happened to each case for which he filed a criminal report, how it ended. It's not the job of the police to follow every trial. So it's a little bit strange, this question. How can the witness be expected to know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the witness who is before us is very much in a position to answer by himself without any counsel taking the floor. This is someone who has conducted important investigations, who had very important responsibilities, and until we get any other reason to think so, he has always been able to answer the questions. So let him answer. And in redirect, if his answer does not suit you, then -- or does not please you, you will have plenty of time to put across what you want to put across. But for the time, being he's answering. So, please, Witness, could you answer the question put to you by Ms. West.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's like this, Ms. West: At this time, I was a civilian. I don't know what was going on in court. I was an ordinary citizen and had been for some time. And when we filed a criminal report about this, we thought that there were sufficient elements for criminal proceedings to be taken against these four persons. From this document, I can see that one of those four men, before that -- or, yes, I will answer.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: I think you misunderstood my question, but let me just ask you a very general question and see if you can help us. For the Trial Chamber to determine the HVO's real commitment to an unbiassed and autonomous judicial system, wouldn't it be better for them to see the number of prosecutions and convictions that the HVO facilitated?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Excuse me. I would object on the grounds that it's up to the Prosecution to show evidence. The burden should not be switched onto the Defence. And that's what -- exactly what the Prosecutor is doing. Where is it that she's gone over there after the last ten years, gotten the evidence, and showing him to try to impeach him on these grounds that nothing was done or that the courts did not work on -- or however the courts were working? It is for the Prosecution, not to use this gentleman. Keeping in mind that when I did try to introduce the Rome Agreement which this office has been working with on the government over there where nothing could be done as of 1995, 1996 -- 1996 onwards, without authorisation from the Prosecution, I was prevented from doing so on the grounds that the gentleman could not comment because it was beyond the point of his employment in the services. Now, however, she wishes to question him about how the courts were functioning well beyond his terms of employment when in fact she hasn't produced one iota or piece of evidence that the courts were not functioning in the manner in which she's describing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. STEWART
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I say, we actually support Mr. Karnavas's objection. Not perhaps precisely -- in precisely the way that he puts it, but that last question by Ms. West isn't an appropriate question for a witness because it's effectively asking for the witness's views on what the correct strategy or tactics should be in the presentation of a case for Your Honours' judgement. And that is not for the witness. It's not really a question of - where I slightly part company with Mr. Karnavas - it's not so much a question of, you know, where the burden of proof is or anything like that, it's -- because once the case is proceeding, everybody's got to do what they can. It's just not a matter for the witness at all. That question is a completely inappropriate question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. West, you know that the witness ceased to work in those services at a certain point in time, and therefore he may not be in a position to answer your question because he was no longer working there. So perhaps you can touch upon this question in a more general nature by asking if a military policeman was aware of the follow-up of decisions that were handed down by tribunals or courts when those courts had been seized. And perhaps he will be in a position to answer, but perhaps he doesn't know that either.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, you heard the Judge's questions. Do you know that information?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All I can say is this: While I was working in the crime department of the military police, our department was a service of the military prosecutor's office, and all our criminal reports filed went towards the Prosecutor. But if we received a request from the Prosecutor back, then we would have to act accordingly.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, let's turn to P03663. And you'll have that, I believe, right in front of you. For everyone else it's in binder 1, part 1. This is a document that you looked at yesterday at the very beginning of the session with counsel for Mr. Coric. That document was a different number, 3651 - I say this is only for the record. Yes. And those questions focused on something else. But this is a document that will be familiar to you, and this is meeting from July 22nd. And it's a meeting with Mr. Coric and the chiefs of the department. And in it you talk about the people at the Heliodrom, and you say: "All those people," and this is the third paragraph, "all those people who have been detained but against whom criminal proceedings have not been initiated are according to the chief of the Military Police Administration unknown to our department. This refers solely to the large number of Muslims who have brought unselectively or indiscriminately to the Heliodrom and you have since been forgotten. And by inertia the crime prevention department has conducted interviews with more than 2.000 people." Go to the next paragraph. It says: "As the head of the Department for Administration and Justice was charged with drawing up a report of the Heliodrom, it follows that according to the decisions of the institutions of this department, it is the duty of the Department of Justice to appoint the warden and make all decisions regarding the detainees." Mr. Vidovic, my question regards this: It appears, from reading this, that you and the people at this meeting, Mr. Coric, were concluding that it was the Department of Justice that was responsible for those detainees. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Ms. West, before I answer, let me give you an explanation. I did not attend this meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: That's fine. But can you tell me, because we spoke about this document on direct, am I correct to say that the conclusion here is that the Department of Justice was responsible for the detainees?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said yesterday and I'll repeat it today, this is a document which I wrote to the prison warden, and I am asking that the --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, my apologies.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- Ministry of Justice -- so yes, yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. So it would appear then that the military police is indicating that instead of itself being responsible for the Heliodrom it's the Department of Justice. Mr. Vidovic, will you confirm for me, in fact, that Mr. Coric appointed the warden, appointed Stanko Bozic as the warden of Heliodrom in December of 1992?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know that, but I think that the answer is no. But as I say, I don't actually know, myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay. I'm going to put this to you and then I'm going to ask you to comment about it. To me this sounds like the military police participants in the meeting know that bad things are going on at the Heliodrom with the Muslims and they're trying to get out of responsibility for what's happening at the prison and find someone else to blame. Would you agree with that? And you can tell me Yes or No or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll say no to that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't agree with your position.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Well let's look at another report and you can tell me if what's stated in it sounds familiar to you. We're going to go to P04841. 4841. It's in the same section. You'll have it right in front of you. This is six weeks later; this is September 6. At this point, the prison situation is --

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you please repeat the number of the document, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And this is a meeting; Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic are at it. And in it they're talking about the detention of persons. And under number 1 they say: "On the basis of verbal reports and insights gained into the manner of executing punishments and conditions of detention of persons captured as active-duty and reserve enemy forces and persons preparing an armed rebellion the situation was declared unsatisfactory and harmful to the reputation and interests of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna. It was also concluded that the responsibility for the present situation does not lie with the HVO." My question to you is, What familiar theme do you see emerging at this meeting as compared to the military police meeting that Mr. Coric attended six weeks earlier?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's very difficult for me to answer because, at the time, this was not the level at which I was working. For most of these people, I only knew who they are. But I simply cannot answer what was going on within the government of the HR HB. I didn't know that at the time. It was a level much higher than the one at which I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vidovic. Judge Antonetti asked you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Ms. West. To make your job easier, let me remind you that you have two minutes left at best, so please try and finish.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President, I will.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Earlier this week the President asked you about who was in a position to free the people at the Heliodrom, and your answer - and I'll quote - was: "I don't know under whose authority they were or who had authority to do that." Now, I'm going to show you some recent testimony in this case.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And if we could have Sanction, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We, Mr. Vidovic, have heard the same response from at least two other witnesses in this courtroom, one of whom was the head of the military -- or was military head commander of the HVO during the period of time when the camps -- you can't hear anything?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't translate.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We don't have a translation. Can you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but --

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you hear it in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In English, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: I can hear the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, can you hear the B/C/S now?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Very good. Okay. So recently we have heard testimony on this issue from Mr. Petkovic and also from Mr. Praljak. And I'd like to look at that testimony. From Mr. Petkovic on March 9th he was asked about who was in charge of the camps on direct examination, and he said: "... everything else was for somebody else to take care of." That was February 17th. He was then asked about it on cross-examination, and he said -- in regard to who was responsible, and he said: "No, it wasn't me, and the Main Staff had nothing to do with that." Mr. Praljak was also asked about this, who was in charge of Heliodrom, and he said: "It was not under the Main Staff. So let me repeat. It's not under the Main Staff, but I can't really tell you under whom it was." So, Mr. Vidovic, my question is this: How is it that you, the head of the military police crime investigative services in Mostar, you were the person who processed these 2.000 plus people into the Heliodrom; you were notified over 60 times in regard to the wounding and killing of the prisoners while they were there; and you facilitated their deportation to third countries; how is it that if you were involved that intimately with the Heliodrom, you didn't know who was responsible for running it?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stick to my statement; I can only extend it partly. Everything I know about Heliodrom was that there was a security platoon of military police which was part of the battalion that I was in, and there was the detention centre administration. These were two men and one female: Mr. Bozic, Mr. Praljak, and a woman. I don't know her name. But I'm not sure under whose command they were. All along I thought that they were under the command of the military judiciary. This is all I can tell you and everything I can say. I did not stay at Heliodrom. I used to come there. I worked there sometimes. But my seat was at the engineering faculty in Mostar and later on it was in Ljubuski. And that is all I can say as an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vidovic. Thank you, Mr. President, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give the floor to the counsel, I have a straightforward follow-up question which is of technical nature. You have just said, Witness, that you thought that the Heliodrom came under the command of the military judiciary. I would like to know this, perhaps you are unable to answer because you are not kept abreast of what is happening in your federation, but I assume that there are military prisons that operate these days. If such military prisons exist, who controls these prisons, the military judiciary, the civilian authorities, the staff of the federation, as things stand today? Are you able to answer this question? If you don't know, I understand full well that you are no longer in charge of these matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't know how this operates today, especially in terms of the military judiciary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Witness. Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, you have the floor. Theoretically, based on our decision, you had 60 seconds left. We actually calculated the seconds. But since you have some time credit, the time you will actually be using now will be deducted from your overall allotted time. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I think that I will be very brief. Could we please give the witness our binder.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take your time. We have the time. Re-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vidovic, first of all I wish to clarify some details of your CV with you. We talked about these things on the first day, but I was warned that some things were not recorded correctly because we had problems with LiveNote. So I wish to go through it again just briefly and only through the details that remained unclear. Is it correct that at the beginning of the war you were a member of the 3rd Cim Battalion of the Mostar HVO?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: The name of the battalion is Cim, C-i-m. And during the time while you were in the military police, you were educated at the faculty of crime science in Zagreb; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: In November 1993, you were in Ljubuski and your task was that you were stand-in chief of the -- you were acting chief of the crime department, but you never became the chief of the department; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: At the same time, in the month of November, you were parallelly following your studies in Zagreb at the institution which I mentioned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please make a pause after I ask you the question. So these were the details of your biography that I wanted to clarify. You have mentioned this several times during the examination in chief, but I wished to reconfirm that. You have told us already that your department, Mostar, was a part of the battalion that was first called the 3rd Battalion and then the 5th Military Police Battalion, and that's how it was throughout the time that you spent in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, I wish to go back briefly to the cross-examination of the Petkovic Defence from pages 51607 and 51608 of the transcript. During the examination-in-chief, which is on pages 51529 and 51530, you said that people from the Heliodrom administration told you that an order had come from Colonel Obradovic that as early as on the next day and onwards you would not be allowed access to Heliodrom and you would not be allowed to interview the people you were investigating. After that, you addressed the operation zone to allow you to do your work. You got the approval, and you continued working. Now, I wish to recollect a few things in connection with this and look at some of the documents briefly. Please look at the first document. That's P03238. In the middle paragraph of this document, in the penultimate sentence, you are talking about this order, and you say that without his signature - and you mean Colonel Obradovic - a visit could not be organised and none of the detainees could be freed from the central military-manned prison, Heliodrom. If I understood you properly, and I see that that's what the document says, did you see this order personally or did you just receive the orders at Heliodrom when you got there to do your work? Can you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were told this at Heliodrom when we got there to work. We were warned that from the next day on we wouldn't be allowed to enter.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next document now. It's P03201. In the previous document you talked about the fact that you wouldn't be able to enter and that without Colonel Obradovic's order no one would be allowed in. This is a document which Mr. Petkovic's Defence presented to you. The date is the 5th of July. We have seen that your document, the previous one, was dated the 6th of July. And here it says: "No one shall be released from your prison without my personal signature." Please tell me, did you have this order in mind when you talked about releasing anyone from the prison in your document?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now please look at the next document. That's P031 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm looking at this order, and I'm trying to understand it. In military terms, there's always a reason for an order to be issued, and here it is stipulated that it is with a view to enforcing order and discipline. That is the grounds for the order. The Defence counsel did not highlight this. Based on this, I have the following question, and I'm sure you'll be able to answer it: As we know, since you have told us, because we have had evidence to that effect, we know that the prison is guarded by military policemen. There are guards standing guard in front of it. So if someone leaves the prison, the guards can be implicated because they are permissive and let the people out. So Colonel Obradovic can issue this order to say that anybody leaving the prison should be vetted by him with his signature. That could be one of the grounds. What do you think of this? Could this be a way of restoring order and discipline by making all the prison wardens aware of the fact that from now onwards anybody leaving the prison should bear the signature of Colonel Obradovic to avoid chaos, disorder, or whatever else occurring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I will remind you that on several occasions I already said that we, the crime department and also the Military Police Platoon that was securing the place, were a part of the Military Police Battalion and each operation zone had one Military Police Battalion as part of its composition. At that moment, Mr. Obradovic, as far as I can remember, was the commander of the operation zone. That is the first part of my answer. And the second part is this: You are right, because if you can remember, I already explained that within the Heliodrom compound there was a number of buildings, only one of which was the prison building. Other buildings housed soldiers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question now: Since we know that there are some detainees that are subject to a committal order, because we know that this is also a civilian prison, can Colonel Obradovic intervene in the way military justice operates and with a committal order of a detainee that has been instructed by a military investigating judge or civil judge or public prosecutor? Can he interfere or intervene in any way? Let me supplement my question: By opposing the departure of someone he had released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's obvious that in this order he acts as someone who is superior to the prison warden at Heliodrom. This is all I can see in this order. And let me repeat, we were informed that unless we did something, on the following day we would not be able to enter and do our work. And that's where all my information about this ended.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, let us just clarify something very briefly. It says down here: "Commander of Sector South." That's above the signature. Was that the position held by Colonel Obradovic at the moment?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if that's what it says, then probably that was what it was. That was probably the sector that became the operation zone later on, but I cannot judge on the exact names, whether it was a sector or the operation zone, but more or less that was it.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell me, do you know if these four prisons which are mentioned here, if they were geographically part of Sector South? I mean, Gabela, Dretelj, Heliodrom, and Ljubuski.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're all to the south of Mostar. So if we follow that logic, then probably they are.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Let us look at P03161, please. It is the next document. And I will remind you that in the previous document with which it all started you talked about visiting the prison, entering the prison, and also release from prison. This is a document from Colonel Obradovic dated the 3rd of July, 1993, and it says: "... I order all visits -- due to the newly arisen situation in the prisons and with the aim of preventing contacts with prisoners during the investigation procedure, I order all visits and access by unauthorised persons to all prisoners in our prisons are forbidden. "All prison administrators are personally answerable to me for the execution of this order." Tell us, is this the order which relates to the part of your testimony in which you told us that you couldn't enter the place?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you please look at the next document now. It's P0 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Witness, were you not an authorised person? You had organically, by your function, you had business to do there. I would assume that you are an authorised person. Apparently that was not the case. Could you explain?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I had an ID card of military police and also a military police badge. At the premises of the Heliodrom prison, they had a list which listed all the members of our department. By this order, Mr. Obradovic placed me and my department among the unauthorised persons. That was why I protested against that in the document dated the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, the next document is P03220, and I'd like us to look at the first page. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] And I'll say for the record that the first page of this document is identical to document P03216, which we haven't included in the binder because it's not necessary. One will suffice.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, this document was also shown to you by the Petkovic Defence. And on page 51608 of the transcript you said that you would like to say three things about this document. However, you weren't given the opportunity during the cross-examination to do so, and I'm going to give you that opportunity now, to put those three points to us. But first of all I'm going to ask you a few short questions. We see at the bottom of there that the document was sent to the wardens of Gabela prison, Dretelj prison, Heliodrom, and Ljubuski. Tell us now, please, do you have any knowledge whatsoever under whose authority the Gabela prison was, as well as the Dretelj prison, in this month of July 1993 when all this was going on? Do you know anything about those two prisons? Just a brief answer, please.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Gabela prison, well, I was never there. All I know is that at that time - you said July 1993 - it was under the control of the brigade called Knez Domagoj, the Knez Domagoj Brigade. That's right. As for Dretelj prison, I think that that, too, was under the control of the brigade. We've explained about Heliodrom several times and a moment ago as well. As for Ljubuski, well, Ljubuski prison, towards the end of 1992, ceased to be a military investigative prison and became a prison of the brigade. And I think that sometime in September 1993 it once again became a military investigative prison. And I know that because of the man who worked there later on, that is to say, Mr. Ivica Kraljevic. So I think that Ljubuski, as of September, came under the control of the military police again. And in the period at the end of 1992 and until September 1993, that it was also under the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, since you said that you never went to Gabela and Dretelj, you said that yesterday, how come you know that?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's my general knowledge, the general information I had going about my business. Just general information.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: When you -- when you say "general information," "going about your business," did you have colleagues who went to those prisons and knew something about them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Exactly. There were people who worked in the crime centres, other ones, and we exchanged information with those centres, working on certain cases, so that's how I came to learn about these two facilities and about the existence of those two prisons.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Vidovic, what three things did you want to say about this document, if you can remember now?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember this document, then under number 1 I would say that there's no heading. And this "military police" that it says here, it's a general concept. And I doubt that a document would reach the Military Police Administration in this form with no header, no year mentioned. And this isn't Mr. Valentin Coric's signature either.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Vidovic. Now, tell me, please, can you remember where you were on the 30th of June, 1993? You said that on that day the BH Army --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I don't know whether Coric's Defence team challenges this document, stating that it is a false document. Irrespective of this, I'm hugely interested in paragraph 3, because when I look at all three paragraphs, it seems, if this document is a true document, that Mr. Coric indicates that the prison is under the jurisdiction of the military police, in other words, under the military authority, because you told us that this was a military judiciary. You told us that the military prison came under the military judiciary. This is what I might be able to understand. And paragraph 3 seems to end -- say to Colonel Obradovic that the prisoners who were captured by the 1st Knez Domagoj Brigade, who don't seem to come under this judiciary, should be released; but if they are released, Colonel Obradovic needs to approve this since he -- they are under his authority and not under the judicial authority. How do you interpret this said paragraph?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you're asking me to interpret just that paragraph, all -- what I can say is that most probably you are thinking, and I can confirm, that they were those disarmed members of the HVO. But, Your Honour, this whole document is a bit suspect, if I can put it that way, and mildly too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, I will slightly correct what you said. I'm not thinking anything; I'm just voicing a hypothesis here. So this is a case that I put to you, but I do not draw any conclusions from this. Counsel, please proceed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] I'd like to remind Your Honours, before I continue, that we challenged the authenticity of this document several times. And as for its authenticity, we conducted cross-examination with a Stojic witness. Slobodan Bozic was his name. And this was recorded in the transcript on 36413 and 36414. That's all I wanted to remind you of.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I asked you whether you remember -- you said that on the 30th of June the attack was launched by the BH Army against the HVO at south -- at North Camp in Mostar. Do you remember where you were, yourself, on the 30th of June?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Mostar on that day in military operations in North Camp. My uncle disappeared. He was an HVO member, and he disappeared on that operation. He was in Zalik Protection Company. And in the next few days I did my best to learn his whereabouts or to learn about what had happened to him generally. Unfortunately, he was killed in those war operations. And those activities of mine went on for the next five or six days, from the 30th of June, which is what you asked me about, onwards.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, on the 30th of June, were you at Heliodrom?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't at Heliodrom on the 30th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, let's take a look at the next document, which is P00352. We're going to skip one and go on to the next. And you have the green stickers, and the pink stickers will indicate the pages we're going to look at in the Croatian and English. It is Josip Praljak's diary. And the pages we're going to look at refer to the 30th of June, 1993. You can see the date in the upper-left-hand corner. Yes, the page number I want us to look at in Croatian is 0354-0197, and in English it is 0354-0197, or page 27. It says here, in the entry for the 30th of June, in the second sentence: "When being arrested, all the organisation about taking these people in and processing them, registering, was taken over by the head of the crime department, Zvonko Vidovic." And then it says who came. And it says: "Bozic: Zvonko, can we take part in this registration process ..." et cetera. Now, you told us a moment ago that on the 30th of June you were not in Heliodrom and explained to us why. Now, Mr. Vidovic, do you have any comment to make with respect to this entry in the diary, and is this true what it says here or not?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not true, because on the 30th of June, I said a moment ago -- I told you what happened to me on the 30th of June, and I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: We finished with the documents now. I just have a few short things to ask you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just -- just a question to make sure, Witness. Can you exclude that you were contacted by telephone or some other means of telecommunication on the 30th of June and answered the question that is mentioned in the diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I remember correctly, and I do believe that I do remember, I spent the whole day, the whole of that day, in the north area of the -- northern area of the town where I was investigating with the soldiers, asking the soldiers who had crossed the Neretva River from North Camp about the fate of my uncle, Dragan Vidovic. I think that I spent -- that I talked to those soldiers until late at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, yesterday, when asked by the Prosecutor, you explained to us how several days after the 30th of June you, under orders from the operative zone, went to Heliodrom and drew up a list of the disarmed members of the HVO who you came across there. And on page 14 of the transcript it says that the -- that the -- you compiled the list on the basis of information given to you by the persons who were there and who had been disarmed. Is that correct? Have I summarised it correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: You also said that you handed the list over to the people in the prison; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell us, please, did you check out the information on the list later on? Did you ever get the list back, or did it remain in the prison?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The service I worked for had nothing more to do with those lists.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Do you know whether the information that the people provided you with, since you didn't check them out later on, do you know whether the information they gave you was correct?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We couldn't know that at the time. We couldn't know whether what they told us was correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell me, please, Mr. Vidovic, do you remember whether in Bosnia-Herzegovina there was general mobilisation in force during this time of war? Do you remember that? Was there an all-out mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that mobilisation had taken place, but I can't say for sure at what point in time it was declared general mobilisation, because my role in the war was as a volunteer in those first days.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Now, regardless of when it was proclaimed - you don't have to know that - who did it encompass? Who were the military conscripts called up when a general mobilisation was declared?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All military-able men above the age of 18 and under the age of 60, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What about women? Were they included in this general mobilisation, if you know?

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. President, I object to these questions. We didn't spoke about mobilisation in the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Counsel, during the cross-examination this issue of mobilisation was never touched upon. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this topic was linked to the cross-examination by the Prosecutor who said that the persons in Heliodrom were civilians. I just want to clear this up, because yesterday during part of the examination we had a situation when I got to my feet and asked what the lists referred to, because we didn't know whether they referred to civilians who were at Heliodrom or soldiers, all of whom had committed crimes, or these disarmed persons. So I'm trying to clarify what it referred to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. If I understand your question correctly, it's to clarify the issue of civilians and military, and it has nothing to do with mobilisation. So very well, please proceed. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: My question was about women. Did women have the duty to respond to the mobilisation call?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Now, the Prosecutor asked you whether the persons disarmed wore different clothing, uniforms, or whatever. Tell me, please, on the basis of clothing, someone's clothing, or whether somebody was wearing a uniform, are you -- would one be able to conclude whether somebody belonged to a unit or not or whether they were a military conscript or not just judging by the clothes they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You couldn't judge that by the clothes they were wearing, who was a civilian and who was a conscript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, that is an important question that is put to you right now. We have a lot of documents talking about military personnel as well as civilians. Given that you were a military policeman, how do you make a distinction between a military person and a civilian? Does a military person carry a military ID card proving that they work for the military? And at the time - I don't know whether it was working - I was wondering whether civilians would carry an ID document proving that they are civilians, or did anyone have to carry -- didn't anyone have to carry any ID documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, every military person had a military ID card. I received my first ID card sometime in May 1992. And everybody who was a regular member of a unit, military unit, was supposed to have an ID indicating the unit to which he belonged, and that was how we could establish whether a soldier -- whether someone was a soldier and which unit they belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may follow up. And can you affirm that these 2.000 persons that were detained in Heliodrom, they all had a military ID card, whether they be men or women?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I can't confirm that. We already said yesterday -- we discussed those persons yesterday when we looked at the lists. They just told us what they wanted, and then we just wrote it down. We couldn't check out whether it was true or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And you did not ask for the military ID card? Because you have now just said that they were not civilians; they were all military, due to the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if somebody had an ID card on them, then they would show it to us, I assume, although I can't remember that now because it's been many years since then. But I assume that if somebody had an ID card, they showed it to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, very quickly, we have seen several documents regarding people that were interviewed by the police, be it the civilian police or the military police, and as far as I can recollect, I can remember that sometimes - perhaps it was all the time, but I could not vouch for that a hundred per cent - we have the name of the person and then we have the ID number. Based on that, when you used to go to the Heliodrom and you would interview those 2.000 people - I'm talking you -- about you, but I know that is also the MUP as well as the SIS - but generally speaking, the work of someone doing the questioning is to ask for the name and the surname, the date of birth, as well as the ID document number. Was that done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we saw in one document that was presented to me, and I remember it, that some persons were questioned in a general manner, and, in addition to other general answers, they would say which unit they belonged to. But, once again, I have to tell you that we only conducted an interview which lasted as long as we needed for the man to say the sentence that was written down; first and last name, date of birth, and current status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course, Witness, but you've seen that when I asked you to read the affirmation - and I'm one of the very few Judges in this Tribunal to proceed this way, and I do it in order to avoid any confusion because I want to be sure that witnesses before us are the correct ones. So I always ask for the name, the surname, the date of birth, the occupation or the profession, and whether they've already testified before a court of law. And I do that systematically. So if I worked for the military police, I would do exactly the same: Name; first name; date of birth; address; and occupation; and also whether they have the status of a military person or a civilian. And if they work for the military, then they should know their ID number, their military ID number. But you are saying that you didn't really do it systematically. This is what I can deduce from what you're saying.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can only answer that as you have seen from many documents and the later inquiries I made on behalf of our service, that that was the duty that was, so to speak, imposed on us. With the few men we had, we had too much work to do anyway within the service that we belonged to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I will not insist on that. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Mr. Vidovic, if I understood you well, I think you have reiterated this several times. These 2.000 persons, what exactly did you do with them? I understood that you made the lists. Not just you, but the whole group that was there. That in the lists you collected their personal information, and you collected the information that each of the persons gave you, and the information included the first and last names, the date of birth, residence, and their status. And they would say what their status was, whether they were soldiers or civilians. Did I say this properly?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. We did not force anyone to tell us anything. If they would state that they were HVO soldiers, we would write down "HVO soldiers." If he said civilian, we would record "civilian." We put down what people told us at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. Did you ask them anything more except these personal -- this personal information? Did you take any statements from them?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Please tell me whether there were any military departments or defence offices in this area which had military records of all able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know about Mostar. There was a military department in Mostar. I suppose that there were military departments that had military records in other places as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell me, did you serve the army in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Before you left to serve the army, did you go through the process that was called recruiting?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Can you tell us who are were all the categories of the population who were obliged to go through this process?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those who went through it were male persons who were adults. And in a medical examination, the degree of their ability would be assessed, both physical and mental, in order to serve army in the JNA at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Vidovic. Now, please tell me, yesterday on several occasions the Prosecutor asked you about lists. I tried to intervene, but then I left it for the redirect because I did not manage to do it then. When you answered questions about lists yesterday, what lists were you talking about? Were these the lists that you talked about today when you were answering my questions, or were there any other lists as well?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I understood your question properly, there were lists in our department, lists of the soldiers against whom we were conducting proceedings and filing criminal reports.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: All right. That was one list. Other lists are the ones that I asked you about just now, the ones with general information about persons detained in Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Did you see any other lists, or are these the lists, these two lists, are these the lists that you were talking about all along yesterday?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: What do you mean "Yes"? You only saw these two lists?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had the lists that we had in my service, and once when we were charged in making the lists which we submitted to Heliodrom.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: And you never saw any other list? You have to say it more loudly.

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Fine. And my last question, Mr. Vidovic: Please tell me, you have lived all your life in Mostar, and you're living there to this day; right?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Tell me, do you move around the -- both the eastern and western bank in Mostar, and what relations do you have with the people in Mostar? Are there any Muslims living there whom you know from the war time and from before the war who are living there now?

utterances.speaker: ZVONKO VIDOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I move through the whole city to this day, and I will answer your question with one single sentence: My daughter is 15, and I taught her one very important thing. She has no ideas about the left and right sides of Mostar or this and that side, as we call them in Mostar. I think I've made it clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MS. WEST
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Vidovic. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I have concluded my questions for this witness. And if you allow me, I would just address the Trial Chamber in three minutes, and that's not connected with the testimony of this witness. We can do it in the presence of the witness or in his absence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we'll escort the witness out of the courtroom. Witness, on behalf of my colleagues, I would like to thank you for having come to The Hague and for having testified on the request of the Coric Defence team. I wish you a good trip back home to your country, and I'm going to ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Counsel. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. On behalf of the Coric Defence and Mr. Coric, I'd like to say the following: We analysed our case constantly, as well as the Prosecution case, and closely analysed and evaluated both the Defence case and the Prosecution case and their exhibits and evidence, our own and that of the other Defence teams, and having consulted Mr. Coric, we consider that we admitted enough -- or, rather, showed enough evidence to show reasonable doubt in the case against our client. We don't intend to explain and go into detail of our decision, but I would like to say that I have the pleasure of announcing that that was the last witness that we intend to call on behalf of the Coric Defence. Your Honours, we would like to thank you for your attention and everybody else in the courtroom, the attention shown to us during our defence case. All I want to say is that that completes our defence case, except that I would like to ask the Trial Chamber to give us until the 24th to submit our motion for documentary evidence, if that is possible. If not, we shall submit it earlier. The date is the 20th of April, by the 20th of April. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I have understood correctly, does this mean that Mr. Coric will not testify and that you have no more witnesses? MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] That's right, Your Honour. Trial -- trial proceedings are a live process. The situation can change from one day to the next depending on how the witnesses testify, what is happening in the courtroom, and so we have weighed all this up and made the decision that we have made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Therefore, Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic, I was looking at the schedule for the months of April. As you know, there will be no hearings next week, and we had planned to resume on the 19th of April -- the 12th of April, I'm sorry, which means that there will be no hearing on the 12th of April. In that case, I would like to turn to Mr. Pusic's Defence counsel. Could we have witnesses on the 12th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. You've given me the floor. I don't think I can do that just now, because if we look at the schedule that we received from the Coric Defence with the 30th of April, well, we didn't think that the Defence case would end today. We thought that Mr. Coric would be testifying. So in the best of cases, we thought we'd start our Defence case at the end of May or the beginning of June. Perhaps if -- we'll do our best to bring in a witness by the 26th of April; that's Variant A. But we haven't yet decided whether we will be presenting a Defence case at all, and we'll give that some more thought. We shall be informing the Court in due course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ibrisimovic, you will have to let us know, because this is of interest to everyone. You will have to inform us very quickly, i.e., whether, (A), you intend to all any witnesses. This is an extremely important point. And if it is the case, if you can call your first witness on the 26th of April already, because we have a slot on the 26th of April. You will, of course, have to see this with Mr. Pusic, which is quite understandable. For the time being, we will wait and see and wait for you to let us know. As soon as you can let us know, we will order -- we will issue a Scheduling Order to indicate when you first witnesses -- witness will take the stand. If you were to tell us that you don't wish to call any witnesses, I believe it would be nonetheless important to have a hearing to address the issue of pre-trial briefs or closing briefs, because you might need some time for that. In that case, we will hold a housekeeping hearing. Mr. Ibrisimovic, you need to let us know whether you intend to call any witnesses; and if you do, when do you intend to do so. And you must let us know.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. I don't know if I've said good afternoon today yet, but good afternoon to everybody in the courtroom as well. I would just like to remind you at this point that we have announced a witness, Momcilo Mandic, and I see that Judge Trechsel is acknowledging -- may I just go into private session for just a moment. I won't keep us long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session let me say this so that it is on the record: Normally speaking, the next witness will come on the 10th of May at a quarter past 2.00. In the meantime, Mr. Ibrisimovic will let us know whether he intends to call witnesses for the defence of Mr. Pusic, something which he intends to do next week. That said, I would like to thank you all. The Court stands adjourned for today.

procedural_notes.text: [The Accused Praljak, Pusic, Petkovic not present]
--- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 4.04 p.m.
